record.paper_title: Electromagnetic probes in heavy-ion collisions: progress and open questions
record.original_question: How can experimental measurements of photons and dileptons produced in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions be made precise enough to use the inclusive electromagnetic signal as a stringent test of nuclear-collision dynamics, despite the fact that electromagnetic observables are experimentally challenging and often have larger uncertainties than hadronic multiplicities, mean transverse momenta, and anisotropic-flow coefficients?

evidence.quote: Photons and dileptons can provide a stringent test of our understanding of nuclear collisions: they probe the parton distribution of the nuclei, the approach to thermal and chemical equilibrium of the system, the plasma’s properties as it expands, its recombination into hadrons, and the final interaction and decays of these hadrons.

On the other hand, photons and dileptons tend to be challenging to measure, and experimental uncertainties are often considerable compared to measurements of hadronic multiplicities, mean transverse momenta, anisotropic coefficients v_n, etc.
Increasing the accuracy of electromagnetic measurements will provide valuable insights into heavy-ion collisions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions, real photons and dileptons (lepton-antilepton pairs from virtual photons) are emitted throughout every stage of the collision: from initial parton scatterings in the colliding nuclei, through the approach to thermal and chemical equilibrium, the expansion of the resulting quark-gluon plasma, hadronization, and the final hadronic rescattering and decays. The inclusive yield of these electromagnetic probes, as a function of transverse momentum, invariant mass, rapidity, centrality, and azimuthal angle (encoded for instance in the anisotropic-flow coefficients v_n obtained from the Fourier decomposition of the azimuthal distribution), therefore offers in principle a stringent constraint on models of the full space-time dynamics of the collision.

In practice, however, experimental measurements of photons and dileptons in heavy-ion collisions are subject to substantial backgrounds (notably from hadronic decays such as π0 → γγ, η → γγ, π0 → γ e+ e−, and conversion electrons) and have statistical and systematic uncertainties that are typically much larger than those of bulk hadronic observables such as charged-particle multiplicities dN/dη, mean transverse momenta ⟨p_T⟩, and anisotropic-flow coefficients v_n of identified hadrons.

Problem. Identify experimental strategies — including detector design, triggering, background subtraction, and analysis techniques — by which the precision of inclusive direct-photon and dilepton measurements (in transverse momentum, invariant mass, and azimuthal anisotropy) in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions can be improved to a level comparable with that of bulk hadronic observables, so that the inclusive electromagnetic signal becomes a quantitatively stringent test of nuclear-collision dynamics across all stages of the collision.
artifact.status_search_result: Improving the precision of direct-photon and dilepton measurements in heavy-ion collisions is an actively pursued goal of the ongoing and upcoming experimental programs at RHIC (sPHENIX, STAR) and the LHC (ALICE 3, upgraded ALICE, CMS, ATLAS), as well as proposed facilities (NA60+, CBM at FAIR). Current measurements still have considerably larger uncertainties than bulk hadronic observables, and the question of how to achieve hadron-level precision is widely regarded as open in the field.

status_evidence.title: ALICE 3 Letter of Intent
status_evidence.snippet: ALICE 3 is designed to deliver precision measurements of thermal dileptons and low-pT direct photons that are not accessible with current detectors.
status_evidence.claim: Precision electromagnetic measurements remain a primary motivation for future detector upgrades, indicating the question is open.

status_evidence.title: NA60+ Letter of Intent
status_evidence.snippet: NA60+ aims at high-precision dimuon and open-charm measurements to study the QGP caloric curve and chiral symmetry restoration.
status_evidence.claim: Future fixed-target programs are being built specifically because current electromagnetic precision is insufficient.

status_evidence.title: sPHENIX physics program
status_evidence.snippet: sPHENIX is designed to extend precision measurements including direct photons and heavy flavor at RHIC.
status_evidence.claim: Active detector programs are pursuing the precision goal, confirming the problem is still open.
